Battle of Stalingrad. The Battle of Stalingrad was a sprawling urban combat from August 1942 to February 1943 between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union for control of a major city on the Volga River. It became the bloodiest battle in history with combined casualties exceeding two million. The German Sixth Army's failure and surrender marked a psychological and military turning point: the first major Axis defeat and the beginning of Soviet momentum that would push Germany back toward Berlin. Stalingrad shattered the myth of German invincibility and galvanized Soviet resolve for the long war ahead.

The fighting took place in and around the industrial city of Stalingrad, modern Volgograd, on the Volga River in southern Russia, a strategic hub for Soviet oil supplies. German Army Group B under General Friedrich Paulus attacked the city as part of Operation Barbarossa's drive toward Soviet oil fields in the Caucasus. Soviet forces, under General Aleksandr Rodimtsev and Georgy Zhukov, were ordered by Stalin to defend the city at any cost with the command: not one step back.

Fighting began in August 1942 with intense house-to-house urban combat as the city was largely reduced to rubble. German forces encircled the city by November 1942, but a Soviet counteroffensive called Operation Uranus from November to December encircled the German Sixth Army instead. Over three hundred thirty thousand Axis troops, mostly German, were trapped in a shrinking pocket as winter set in with supply lines cut and starvation setting in.

Paulus and the remnants of the Sixth Army surrendered on February 2, 1943, with fewer than six thousand German prisoners surviving Soviet captivity. German morale collapsed and Soviet morale soared as the Axis lost the initiative on the Eastern Front permanently. Stalingrad became a symbol of Soviet sacrifice and resilience, inspiring propaganda and historical memory on both sides. Stalingrad represents the moment when the Second World War's trajectory fundamentally shifted and the Soviet Union became clearly ascendant.
